source.title: How Does Learning Rate Decay Help Modern Neural Networks
source.authors: Kai-Chao You; Mingsheng Long; Jian-Min Wang; Michael I. Jordan

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present, though some plots and table formatting are flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies learning-rate decay and reports optimization and generalization outcomes, using a different intervention from the listed claim versions. It does not test any version's named conditions or measures.
record.gate_note: The paper reports cited results from other work and uses plot-based results for several of its own experiments. Cited results are excluded. The measured Hessian eigenvalues are not a measure of the training–test gap, and the transferability experiments concern cross-dataset transfer, which the claim excludes.
record.test_reason: The study tests explanations of learning-rate decay, not V1–V8. Its noise experiment does not compare near-perfect fitting of fully random labels with natural-label held-out performance; its GD/SGD experiments do not isolate batch size under a fixed epoch budget; its Hessian spectrum does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness against generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' conclusion: they propose that an initially large learning rate suppresses noisy-data memorization and subsequent decay enables complex-pattern learning. PS10 experiments provide direct evidence; real-world transfer experiments provide indirect support through an implication of that explanation.
record.recipe_differences: Studies learning-rate decay effects and pattern complexity; the listed versions focus on memorization/generalization, architecture, optimizers, batch size, dropout, sharpness, or memorized-example removal.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning-rate decay timing changes the reported generalization outcome between the Gradient Descent and SGD experiments; the SGD comparison includes a no-decay condition.

fits_no_version.finding: Learning-rate decay yields negligible optimization or generalization benefit for full-batch GD on CIFAR-10, but improves test accuracy for SGD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of learning-rate decay depends on the training algorithm in these WideResNet experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: AutoDecay reaches 75.91% top-1 and 92.81% top-5 accuracy in 81 epochs, versus 75.80% and 92.76% in 90 epochs for StepDecay.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss-triggered learning-rate decay can shorten this ImageNet training run while preserving accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: On PS10 with 10% noise, an initially large learning rate followed by decay suppresses noisy-data fitting and improves complex-pattern accuracy relative to a constant small learning rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning-rate schedules can change the balance between noisy-data memorization and complex-pattern learning.

fits_no_version.finding: Stage-3 incremental transferability is lower than stage-2 transferability on all four target datasets under both transfer strategies. Sketch250 stage-3 transferability is negative only with fixed features (-0.06); with finetuning it remains positive (0.11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Later ImageNet training stages yield less transferable incremental gains, with effects depending on the target dataset and transfer strategy.

record.problems: Several key comparisons are reported only through plots, without exact values or uncertainty estimates. The paper itself notes that pattern complexity in real-world datasets is intractable and validates its explanation there through transferability as an indirect implication.
record.rows_left_out: Section 5, Figures 9 and 10: pattern-specific accuracy curves on PS10, including the 10%-noise condition, are figure-only and not directly reported as a training–test gap. Section 6, Figure 11 and Table 2: cross-dataset transferability and accuracies are omitted because out-of-distribution transfer is separate from the claim. Section 4.1, Figure 5: Hessian eigenvalues are omitted because they do not measure the claimed training–test gap.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fixed-random-label fitting alongside natural-label generalization using the same architecture and recipe, and chance held-out accuracy with random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and whether adapted recipes remove their penalty.
Dropout comparisons, training-set-size dependence, and interactions with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus generalization gaps at similarly low training loss, including comparison with norm and margin measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts apply to V1–V8. The record's T2 classification contradicts its own statement that no version is tested. Its transfer finding also overstates the negative Sketch250 result by omitting the fixed-feature condition.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare fitting fixed random labels with natural-label generalization or evaluate held-out accuracy on random labels.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.
Uses SGD and gradient descent, not a comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with norm- or margin-based measures.
Does not identify or remove memorized training examples.

rows.subject: WideResNet
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR10 with Gradient Descent; learning-rate decay timing varied and compared with no decay.
rows.value: Authors report that decay brings negligible benefit to optimization or generalization; final performances are almost the same regardless of decay timing.
rows.note: The description gives the outcome but not exact plotted values.
rows.check: The reported negligible decay benefit is accurate, but establishes absence of a learning-rate-decay effect, not absence of any listed version. Training loss and test accuracy are bundled into one row.

rows.subject: WideResNet
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR10 with SGD using several learning-rate decay timings, including no decay.
rows.value: The best performances before and after decay differ by a noticeable margin; without decay, performance plateaus and oscillates, with no chance of reaching the post-decay performance shown in the other columns.
rows.note: The text describes the comparison; exact values are only plotted.
rows.check: The reported test-accuracy improvement after decay is accurate but measures none of V1–V8.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: ImageNet training with AutoDecay compared with StepDecay; the only stated change is the learning-rate strategy.
rows.note: Authors state that AutoDecay shortened training time by 10% without hurting performance and brought a slight improvement.
rows.check: This is the authors' AutoDecay method-performance comparison, not a claim-testing row. The accuracies are correct; the baseline uses 90 epochs and AutoDecay 81. Split top-1 and top-5 if retained. The displayed result is Figure 14, although the prose calls it Table 14.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
